title: RCC RefCert: A Research Toolkit for Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity
description:
A source may already supply a qubit in a pure state. Preparing that same state from a maximally mixed qubit requires removing entropy. Reference-Contingent Complexity (RCC) takes structural fairness as a physical postulate. The structure supplied by the background sets the zero point for complexity, and the resources used to generate additional structure count toward preparation cost.

RCC RefCert is a research toolkit for structure-fair quantum circuit complexity. You can build a finite-control model for your system and verify its reference certificate. Once the admissible model and target accuracy are fixed, information from the final state gives a rigorous lower bound on optimal preparation cost. A single certificate can rule out every circuit below that cost, even when the preparation history is unknown. You can also compare candidate preparations and use window RCC to study subsystem complexity in pure and mixed states.

Code and guides · PyPI package · RCC paper

Research tasks

  • Models and reference certificates. Specify quantum channels, a reference state and control rules. Calculate terminating program outputs, construct numerical certificate candidates for stable models and check reference domination.
  • Terminal-state lower bounds. Use an exact target spectrum or observed counts from a projection measurement specified in advance. For measured counts, the report gives the sampling confidence alongside the bound.
  • Preparation costs. In exact diagonal-preserving models, combine a rigorous lower bound with the cost of a successful candidate to bound the optimum. For numerical matrix models, compare each candidate’s cost and trace distance from the target.
  • Subsystem complexity. Use window RCC to compare subsystems at a common reference and control bandwidth. Separate local and correlation contributions or follow them along a preparation.
  • Independent verification. Share the inputs and results of a model, certificate, cost or window calculation in a bundle that another researcher can recompute.
  • Reproduce calculations from the RCC paper. Compare fresh results for the reference cases with the archived data and report. The guide to the equations and code shows where each calculation is implemented.

Worked examples

  • A one-qubit reset gives a one-slot lower bound and a preparation that attains it. The algorithmic cooling example shows how to read an interval when the lower and upper bounds differ.
  • Bell pairs and a GHZ state have the same global spectrum. Their subsystem complexity profiles distinguish how correlations are distributed. Other editable probes follow phase noise and cooling. The three notebooks include inputs you can adapt to your own model or state.

Run and share a calculation

With Python 3.10 or newer, install the package and run the four-qubit reset example in a new working directory.

python -m pip install "rcc-refcert==0.3.0"
python -m rcc_refcert cost template cyclic-reset > task.json
python -m rcc_refcert cost analyze task.json --bundle task.rccbundle

The preparation-cost interval is [5,5] atomic slots. Every successful program needs at least five slots, and one reaches the target in exactly five, including the halt operation. To try a different target or tolerance, edit task.json and choose a new bundle filename.

Anyone with the package and the saved bundle can verify the calculation by running

python -m rcc_refcert bundle verify task.rccbundle

To reproduce the paper’s reference cases, run

python -m rcc_refcert reproduce --check

Expect three MATCH checks for the reference expectations, data and report.

Cost and window reports support text, JSON and Markdown. The export guide also shows how to save subsystem profiles as CSV or plot them.

Interpreting the results

A preparation-cost interval refers to the stated model, target, tolerance and atomic cost. A numerical matrix check uses the chosen tolerance. Window RCC measures the complexity of a reduced state relative to the reference and control scale. A finite-accuracy lower bound on preparation cost also uses the model inputs and one-shot corrections. The scientific scope gives the definitions and assumptions.

The RCC paper also discusses high-energy physics. Its generation-cost bounds can be compared with the complexity–volume and complexity–action conjectures for boundary states when the preparation task and resource conventions match.

Version 0.3.0 adds preparation-cost intervals and subsystem complexity profiles. Both workflows now support analysis bundles for independent verification. See the changelog for changes and compatibility.
